author: Francis Fukuyama
introFa: کتاب «The End of History and the Last Man» نوشته Francis Fukuyama یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The End of History and the Last Man»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: 329 complacent: ’The economy, stupid!’ is the slogan that put a Democrat back in the White House. Americans are concerned about their jobs, loss of health insurance when out of work, national economic decline, and the future of their children when still more of their consumer goods are made overseas, chiefly by American corporations manufacturing in cheap- labour countries. They are worried about guns and drugs; about child sex abuse; about a murder rate at least five times that of Western Europe; about the homeless; about race relations; about chemical, biological and nuclear pollution; about a daily diet of food preservatives, fertilizers and insecticides; about the greenhouse effect and skin cancer from erosion of the ozone layer; and (some of them) about the imminent end not just of history but of the world. When they try to remedy these problems they are frustrated by the special interests and political lobbies, who fund politicians on both sides in the expectation of government contracts, subsidies, protective legislation, and vetos on taxation and reform. Far from thinking they have reached a nirvana of political perfection, most Americans, decent, bien pensant people who wish the best for themselves and the world, hope against hope for a fairer society and a better world for their children. Only reactionaries like Fukuyama, an ex-official of the Reagan-Bush State Department, and his masters want to stop the clock where Reagan and Bush left it, in the hope that expensive social change can be halted. If this is the end of the history, 62 per cent of Americans believe in and voted for a new beginning. Secondly, Fukuyama fails to analyse either democracy or the free market, and assumes that the American model is the same as but better than the rest. He seems unaware that other Western democracies, as those Americans calling for a national health service admit, have passed further along the road to responsible democracy, or that the successor states of the Soviet empire look not to the United States but to the German ’social market’, Scandinavian social democracy, or Japanese ’managed capitalism’ for their model. Worldwide, the free market is free mainly for multinational corporations, a sophisticated version of the mercantile camaraderie that Adam Smith expressly warned against. Thirdly, and more profoundly, Fukuyama misconstrues Hegel, his revered but transduced guru. Hegel’s thymos was not simply a desire for equal recognition. It was a demand, the feudal lord’s or the Mafia godfather’s, for more than equal recognition, in other words for power over others. Hence the talk of masters and slaves. The logic of this is that from the moment egalitarian democracy comes into existence the powerful and the rich, the strong and the cunning-Pareto’s lions and foxes-look for ways to re-establish mastery. ’Positional goods’ like power and privilege, honour and respect, cannot be equally shared with- out becoming worthless. Democracy is not a static but a dynamic con- dition : the price of liberty is eternal vigilance, a never-ending battle to 28, 2015 at UNIV OF OKLAHOMA LIBRARIES on March ehq.sagepub.com

330 prevent the greedy and power-hungry from exploiting the rest, an ongoing political task that takes all the moral intelligence and institutional ingen- uity of the people. It needs to defend itself not only from external and home-grown marauders but also, since its demands include the civil rights of individuals and minorities, from the tyranny of the majority. Fuku- yama, like Hayek, would freeze-dry it in its present imperfection and deny any change a hearing. Finally, and fundamentally, Fukuyama’s thesis is bedevilled by the intellectualist fallacy, the real (pace Julien Benda) trahaison des clercs. Intellectuals’ desire for recognition leads them to overvalue theorists and claim that they are more influential than they are. In their favoured model a great thinker thinks, and converts disciples, who then spread his gospel to the hoi polloi. In fact, the reverse is more often true: people choose gurus who tell them what they want to hear; they select what ’speaks to their condition’. The Adam Smith of the free marketeers bears little resemblance to the author of The Wealth of Nations. The same people would believe in their crude and, under corporate capitalism, unreal version of the free market if Adam Smith, Milton Friedman and Friedrich von Hayek had never written a word. Fukuyama’s Hegel is very different from, say, that of Pareto, who would see in him merely the ’residues’ of a government-employed academic serving military aristocrats transmogrified into the unheroic bureaucrats of an authoritarian state. Fukuyama thinks he is explicating Hegel, but the practical effect is to tell far-right politicians and big business men what they want to hear. He is the ’beamish boy’ of American conservatism, and deserves to be clasped to the bosom of the triumphalist establishment. John Lukacs is an outsider too, a Hungarian-American of more inde- pendent mind. He has no love either for Soviet Communists or American anti-Communists, both of whom he categorizes as false patriots who made a good thing out of the Cold War and regret its passing. His book, despite its pretentious title, is a modest essay on our present discontents, a pot-pourri of reflections on international history and travels around post-Cold War Europe. Its major thesis, that the twentieth century lasted only from 1914 to 1989 and was characterized not by the titanic struggle between Communism and capitalism but by the tribal nationalism which is still demoralizing the whole world, is covered in the first nine-page chapter. Its minor one, that the modem Eurocentric world which began with the Columbian conquests is now in terminal decline, chiefly occupies the last twenty pages. The rest of the book is exegesis and repetition, interspersed with charming vignettes from his travel diaries around post- 1989 Eastern Europe. Shrewder and more realistic than Fukuyama, Lukacs takes a more jaundiced view of capitalist democracy and the free market: ’Capitalism. as well as parliamentary liberalism, were nineteenth-century phenomena 28, 2015 at UNIV OF OKLAHOMA LIBRARIES on March ehq.sagepub.com

331 with little relevance to the twenty-first, with its current realities being obscured by an outdated vocabulary of economists.’ Though he does not quote Hegel, he understands his thesis better: ’The great and enduring problems are political, not economic. They involve lust and power, not money.’ He does not buy the naive notion that the ex-Communist coun- tries are yearning for American-type democracy and capitalism. They are, to his chagrin, replacing one kind of state bureaucracy with another, run by the same kind of people. Already they are installing effectively one-party regimes and treating dissidents and opposition politicians as pariahs, if not traitors. Like Hitler and Stalin before them, they are nationalists first, ideologues only when it serves their purpose. The tyr- anny of the majority, or those who claim to speak for the majority, is rising like the phoenix from the ashes of 1989. Even in the West, democracy is mocked by the perquisites and trap- pings of power: the imperial presidency or premiership, the Ruritanian ceremonial and uniforms, exclusive accommodation and furnishings, chauffeur-driven cars, servile aides, VIP travel, all the grovelling defer- ence beyond the reach of the merely rich, are creating an irresponsible elite as corrupt as the Soviet nomenklatura that brought down the Com- munist empire. Under the pretense of popular sovereignty the power of the state is abused for private pomp and gain; hence ’the increasing inefficiency of and impatience with parliamentary rule’. In Eastern Europe democracy is in grave danger; in the West it is looking very sick. Far from being the triumphant culmination of history, capitalist democracy may be nearing the end of its shelf-life. Neither Lukacs nor Fukuyama squarely faces the greatest threats to the twenty-first century world: the population explosion, global warming, erosion of the ozone layer, and the competition for food, fuel and resources which may plunge mankind into bloody wars between growingly affluent North and increasingly impoverished South. If-or when?-these problems come to the boil, what price liberal democracy and the free market then? Fukuyama is right that the direction of history cannot be reversed without catastrophe. Unfortunately for this reckless and irresponsible generation, that does not make it impossible. Will ’the end of history’ then have a sinister and more terminal meaning? Harold Perkin Northwestern University 28, 2015 at UNIV OF OKLAHOMA LIBRARIES on March ehq.sagepub.com
